title: Bēowulf
titleEn: Beowulf — Fitt XLI: Ravenswood and the Curse (lines 2946–3057)
part: Fitt XLI · Ravenswood and the Curse (lines 2946–3057)
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 111–115, lines 2946–3057 (fitt XLI). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t:
Wæs sīo swātswaðu Sw[ē]ona ond Gēata,
wælrǣs weora wīde gesȳne,
hū ðā folc mid him fǣhðe tōwehton.
sentences.l: Was the blood-track of Swedes and Geats, the slaughter-rush of men, widely seen — how the peoples between them awakened the feud.
sentences.i: The trail of blood that Swedes and Geats left, the rush of slaughter among their men, could be seen far and wide, and it was plain how the two peoples had stirred up the feud between them.
sentences.n: The messenger’s speech, begun at 2900, goes on with the story of the Swedish war that he began in the previous part. ‘Wæs sīo swātswaðu … wælrǣs … gesȳne’ is ‘was the blood-track, the slaughter-rush, seen’: ‘swāt’ ‘blood’ + ‘swaðu’ ‘track’; ‘wælrǣs’ is ‘slaughter-rush’ (‘rǣs’, a charge); ‘weora’ is the genitive plural of ‘wer’ ‘man’. ‘Gesȳne’ is ‘seen, visible’. ‘Hū ðā folc … tōwehton’ is ‘how the peoples awakened the feud between them’: ‘tōwehton’ is the past plural of a verb ‘tōweccan’, from ‘weccan’, ‘wake, rouse’ (the past of ‘weccan’ is ‘wehte’), which I take as ‘stir up’ (a guess at the compound; Trautmann reads ‘geworhton’, ‘made’). The ‘ē’ of ‘Sw[ē]ona’ is added: the manuscript has ‘swona’, and the Thorkelin reading in the apparatus is the one printed.

sentences.l: Went then the good one with his companions, old, very sorrowful, to seek a stronghold; the earl Ongentheow turned higher up;
sentences.i: Then the old Swedish king, sorrowing deeply, withdrew with his followers to look for a stronghold; the earl Ongentheow turned away up the slope;
sentences.n: ‘Gewāt him … fæsten sēcean’ is ‘went (himself) … to seek a stronghold’: ‘gewāt’ is the past of ‘gewītan’, ‘him’ is a reflexive dative, and ‘fæsten’ is the object of ‘sēcean’. ‘Se gōda’ is Ongentheow, king of the Swedes (the form is ‘Ongenþīo’ here and ‘Ongenðīow’ at 2961). The poet gives the enemy king the very word used for Higelac at 2944, ‘the good one’. ‘Frōd’ is ‘old and wise’, ‘felageōmor’ ‘very sorrowful’ (‘fela’ is an adverb, ‘much’). ‘Gædelingum’ is ‘companions’. ‘Ufor’ is ‘higher, further up’, and ‘oncirde’ the past of ‘oncirran’, ‘turn’; I take it as ‘turned back up the hill’ toward his fort.

sentences.t:
hæfde Higelāces hilde gefrūnen,
wlonces wīgcræft;
sentences.l: He had learned of Higelac’s fight, the proud one’s war-craft;
sentences.i: He had heard of Higelac’s fighting, of the proud king’s skill in war;
sentences.n: ‘Hæfde … gefrūnen’ is ‘had learned by asking’, the past participle of ‘gefrignan’ with ‘hæfde’ (a pluperfect). ‘Higelāces hilde’ is ‘Higelac’s battle’, and ‘wlonces wīgcræft’ ‘the proud one’s war-craft’, the genitive ‘wlonces’ being Higelac again. Ongentheow’s fear of that name explains the retreat.

sentences.t:
wiðres ne trūwọde,
þæt hē sǣmannum onsacan mihte,
heaðolīðendum hord forstandan,
bearn ond brȳde;
sentences.l: in resistance he did not trust, that he could withstand the seamen, defend the hoard against the battle-farers, children and brides;
sentences.i: He had no faith that he could resist the seafarers, or defend his treasure, his children and his wives against these men of battle;
sentences.n: ‘Wiðres ne trūwọde’ is ‘in resistance he did not trust’: ‘trūwian’ takes the genitive, and ‘wiðre’ is ‘resistance’. The dot under the ‘ọ’ in ‘trūwọde’ is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre; it changes nothing in the sense. ‘Sǣmannum’ is ‘seamen’ and ‘heaðolīðendum’ ‘battle-farers’ (‘līðan’ ‘travel’, ‘heaðo-’ ‘battle’), both datives, both the Geats, who came by sea; ‘onsacan’ takes the dative ‘sǣmannum’, and ‘forstandan’ takes the accusative of what is defended (‘hord’, ‘bearn’, ‘brȳde’) with the dative ‘heaðolīðendum’ of those defended against. ‘Bearn ond brȳde’ is ‘children and brides’, the things Ongentheow fears to lose with the hoard; ‘brȳd’ means woman, wife.

sentences.t:
bēah eft þonan
eald under eorðweall.
sentences.l: he bowed, back from there, old, under the earth-wall.
sentences.i: So the old man turned back from there and went in under his earthen rampart.
sentences.n: ‘Bēah eft þonan’ is ‘bowed (turned) back from there’: ‘bēah’ is the past of ‘būgan’, here ‘bend, turn away, retreat’. ‘Eorðweall’ is ‘earth-wall’, a rampart of heaped earth, the fort’s defence. The subject, Ongentheow, is carried over from 2951.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs ǣht boden
Swēona lēodum, segn Higelāce[s]
freoðowong þone forð ofereōdon,
syððan Hrēðlingas tō hagan þrungon.
sentences.l: Then was pursuit proclaimed to the Swedes’ people; the standard of Higelac went forth over that peace-field, after the Hrethlings pressed to the enclosure.
sentences.i: Then the chase was proclaimed upon the Swedish people, and Higelac’s banner advanced across the ground around the fort, once the Hrethlings had pushed up to the stronghold.
sentences.n: ‘Ǣht’ I take as ‘pursuit’, so ‘ǣht boden’ is ‘pursuit was proclaimed’, with ‘Swēona lēodum’ a dative, ‘to (upon) the Swedes’ people’; that is a guess from the sense (Holthausen reads ‘ōht’, ‘terror’, and Sievers ‘sæcc’, ‘strife’, for ‘segn’). ‘Higelāce[s]’: the final ‘s’ is added by editors, the manuscript having ‘Higelāce’, and ‘segn’ is singular with a plural verb ‘ofereōdon’, as if the banner meant the men under it; I take it so. Other editors put the stop after ‘Higelāce(s)’ instead of before ‘segn’, which attaches ‘segn Higelāces’ to the words before it. ‘Freoðowong’ is ‘peace-field’, which I take as the cleared ground that was meant to protect the fort (a guess). ‘Hrēðlingas’ are Hrethel’s kin, the Geats; ‘hagan’ is the ‘enclosure’ of 2892, here the fort.

sentences.t:
Þǣr wearð Ongenðīow ecgum sweorda,
blondenfexa on bid wrecen,
þæt se þēodcyning ðafian sceolde
Eafores ānne dōm.
sentences.l: There was Ongentheow, the blended-haired one, by the edges of swords driven to a stand, so that the people-king had to consent to Eofor’s one decree.
sentences.i: There, hard pressed by the edges of swords, the grey-haired Ongentheow was driven to stand at bay, so that the king of his people had to bow to the will of Eofor alone.
sentences.n: ‘Þǣr wearð … wrecen’ is ‘there was driven’, the passive of ‘wrecan’; ‘on bid wrecen’ is ‘driven to a stand’ (‘bid’, a waiting, a holding out), and ‘ecgum sweorda’ ‘with the edges of swords’. The ‘a’ of ‘sweorda’ is Klaeber’s: the manuscript has ‘sweordū’ and Kemble gave ‘sweorda’. ‘Blondenfexa’ is ‘the blended-haired one’ (‘blonden’, ‘blended, mixed’, + ‘fexa’, the weak form of ‘feax’, ‘hair’), which I take as ‘grey-haired’, as in ‘blondenfeax’ at 1791 and ‘blondenfeaxum’ at 1873 (the colour is a guess from the mixing). ‘Ðafian sceolde’ is ‘had to consent to’, and ‘Eafores ānne dōm’ ‘Eofor’s one decree’: the old king’s fate lay with Eofor alone. Eofor appears as ‘Eafores’ here and ‘Iofore’ at 2993.

sentences.t:
Hyne yrringa
Wulf Wonrēding wǣpne gerǣhte,
þæt him for swenge swāt ǣdrum sprong
forð under fexe.
sentences.l: Him angrily Wulf Wonred’s son reached with a weapon, so that for the blow the blood sprang from his veins, forth under his hair.
sentences.i: Wulf, son of Wonred, struck him in anger with his weapon, so that under the blow the blood sprang from the veins, forth from beneath his hair.
sentences.n: ‘Hyne … wǣpne gerǣhte’ is ‘reached him with a weapon’ (‘gerǣcan’ with the accusative). ‘Wonrēding’ is the patronymic, ‘son of Wonred’; Wulf is Eofor’s brother, as 2978 shows. ‘Yrringa’ is an adverb, ‘angrily’. ‘For swenge’ is ‘for (because of) the blow’; ‘ǣdrum’ is the dative plural of ‘ǣdre’, ‘vein’, so the blood sprang ‘from the veins’. ‘Fexe’ is ‘hair’ (dative), and the hurt is therefore to Ongentheow’s head.

sentences.t:
Næs hē forht swā ðēh,
gomela Scilfing, ac forgeald hraðe
wyrsan wrixle wælhlem þone,
syððan ðēodcyning þyder oncirde.
sentences.l: Not was he afraid, however, the old Scylfing, but repaid quickly that slaughter-blow with a worse exchange, after the people-king turned thither.
sentences.i: Yet he was not afraid, the old Scylfing, but swiftly paid back that deadly blow with a worse one in exchange, when the king turned on him.
sentences.n: ‘Næs hē forht swā ðēh’ is ‘he was not afraid, however’. ‘Scilfing’ is a member of the Scylfing house, the Swedish kings, and the poet calls Ongentheow ‘gomela’, ‘the old one’. ‘Forgeald … wyrsan wrixle’ is ‘repaid with a worse exchange’: ‘wrixle’ (‘exchange’) is a dative of means. ‘Wælhlem’ is ‘slaughter-blow’ (‘hlem’ a crash, a blow). ‘Þyder oncirde’ is ‘turned thither’, toward Wulf.

sentences.t:
Ne meahte se snella sunu Wonrēdes
ealdum ceorle ondslyht giofan,
ac hē him on hēafde helm ǣr gescer,
þæt hē blōde fāh būgan sceolde,
fēoll on foldan;
sentences.l: Could not the keen son of Wonred give a return-blow to the old churl, but he had first cut through the helmet on his head, so that, blood-stained, he had to bow, fell to the ground;
sentences.i: The bold son of Wonred could not return the blow to the old man, for Ongentheow had already split the helmet on his head, so that, stained with blood, he had to bend, and fell to the ground;
sentences.n: ‘Ne meahte … ondslyht giofan’ is ‘could not give a return-blow’; ‘ondslyht’ is ‘answering blow’, and ‘ealdum ceorle’ is ‘to the old churl’, a dative, ‘ceorl’ here just ‘man’. The italic ‘o’ is Klaeber’s change; the apparatus only points back to a note at 2929 that is not in this packet, so I cannot say what the manuscript has. ‘Ac hē him … ǣr gescer’ is ‘but he had cut it first’: ‘hē’ is Ongentheow, ‘him’ Wulf, ‘gescer’ the past of ‘gescieran’, ‘cleave’. ‘Fāh’ here is ‘stained’. ‘Būgan sceolde’ is ‘had to bow, give way’, and ‘fēoll on foldan’ ‘fell to the ground’.

sentences.t:
næs hē fǣge þā gīt,
ac hē hyne gewyrpte, þēah ðe him wund hrine.
sentences.l: not was he doomed yet, but he recovered himself, though a wound touched him.
sentences.i: But he was not doomed yet; he recovered himself, though the wound had struck him.
sentences.n: ‘Næs hē fǣge’ is ‘he was not fey’, doomed to die; the poet marks that Wulf’s hour was not yet. ‘Gewyrpte’ is the past of ‘gewyrpan’, ‘recover’, with the reflexive ‘hyne’. ‘Þēah ðe him wund hrine’ is ‘though a wound touched him’: ‘hrine’ is a past subjunctive of ‘hrīnan’ (the short ‘i’ is the past stem) with the dative ‘him’, and ‘wund’ the subject.

sentences.t:
Lēt se hearda Higelāces þegn
brād[n]e mēce, þā his brōðor læg,
ealdsweord eotonisc entiscne helm
brecan ofer bordweal; ðā gebēah cyning,
folces hyrde, wæs in feorh dropen.
sentences.l: Let the hard thane of Higelac, when his brother lay, the broad sword, the old sword, ettinish, break the giant-made helmet over the shield-wall; then the king bowed, the people’s herdsman, was dropped into the life.
sentences.i: Then the hardy thane of Higelac, while his brother lay on the ground, let his broad sword, an ancient blade of giants’ make, break the giant-made helmet across the shield-rim; and the king, the shepherd of his people, bent and was struck to the quick.
sentences.n: ‘Lēt … brecan’ is ‘let (made) break’ (‘lǣtan’ with an accusative and infinitive): ‘brād[n]e mēce’, with ‘ealdsweord eotonisc’ in apposition, is the thing that breaks, and ‘entiscne helm’, ‘giant-made helmet’, is the object of ‘brecan’ (Sievers, Holthausen and Sedgefield insert ‘þā’ after ‘Lēt’). The thane, ‘Higelāces þegn’, is Eofor, named at 2993; ‘his brōðor’ is Wulf. ‘Brād[n]e mēce’ is ‘broad sword’ (the ‘n’ is added: the manuscript has ‘brade’), and ‘ealdsweord eotonisc’ ‘old sword, ettinish’ (‘eotonisc’, ‘of giants’), in apposition. ‘Bordweal’ is ‘shield-wall’, which I take as the rim of Ongentheow’s shield or the line of his guards (a guess). ‘Gebēah’ is ‘bowed, sank’. ‘Wæs in feorh dropen’ is, word for word, ‘was dropped into the life’: ‘dropen’ is the participle of ‘drēopan’, ‘drip, drop, fall’, and ‘in feorh’ ‘into the life’. The sense ‘mortally struck’ is from the context, and the whole phrase is a guess.

sentences.t:
Ðā wǣron monige, þē his mæg wriðon,
ricone ārǣrdon, ðā him gerȳmed wearð,
þæt hīe wælstōwe wealdan mōston.
sentences.l: Then there were many who bound his kinsman, quickly raised him up, when room was made for them, that they might hold the slaughter-place.
sentences.i: Then many were there who bound up his kinsman’s wounds and quickly set him on his feet, when the way was cleared for them and they could take control of the field of the slain.
sentences.n: ‘Þē his mæg wriðon’ is ‘who bound his kinsman’: ‘wriðon’ is the past plural of ‘wrīðan’, ‘bind’ (bandage), and ‘mæg’ is Wulf. ‘Ricone ārǣrdon’ is ‘quickly raised up’. ‘Ðā him gerȳmed wearð’ is ‘when room was made for them’: ‘gerȳman’ ‘clear’, the passive. ‘Wælstōwe wealdan mōston’ is ‘might rule (have control of) the slaughter-place’; ‘wealdan’ takes a genitive or dative, and ‘mōston’ is the past plural of ‘mōtan’, ‘be allowed’ (the ending does not show indicative or subjunctive).

sentences.t:
Þenden rēafode rinc ōðerne,
nam on Ongenðīo īrenbyrnan,
heard swyrd hilted, ond his helm somod;
hāres hyrste Higelāce bær.
sentences.l: While one warrior plundered the other, took from Ongentheow the iron byrnie, the hard sword hilted, and his helmet too; the grey one’s trappings he bore to Higelac.
sentences.i: While one man stripped the other, taking from Ongentheow his iron mail-coat, his hard hilted sword and his helmet as well, he carried the grey king’s gear to Higelac.
sentences.n: ‘Þenden rēafode rinc ōðerne’ is ‘while one warrior plundered the other’, the warrior Eofor and the ‘ōðerne’ Ongentheow. ‘Īrenbyrnan’ is ‘iron byrnie’ (‘byrne’, mail-shirt), ‘heard swyrd hilted’ ‘hard sword hilted’ (‘hilted’ an adjective, ‘with a hilt’), ‘somod’ ‘together, too’. ‘Hāres hyrste’ is ‘the grey one’s trappings’, ‘hār’ in the genitive and ‘hyrste’ an accusative plural. Higelac’s share in the winning is the point: the arms go to him, and he pays for them.

sentences.t:
Hē ð(ām) frætwum fēng ond him fægre gehēt
lēana (mid) lēodum, ond gelǣste swā;
sentences.l: He received the trappings and fairly promised him rewards among the people, and he performed so;
sentences.i: Higelac accepted the gear and promised Eofor handsome rewards before the people, and he was as good as his word;
sentences.n: ‘Hē’ is Higelac; ‘fēng’ is the past of ‘fōn’, ‘take’, with the dative ‘ð(ām) frætwum’, ‘the trappings’. The ‘ām’ is restored in parentheses, because the manuscript is lost there (Grundtvig’s transcript supplies it). ‘Him’ is most likely Eofor, who brought the gear (both brothers are named two lines on), and ‘fægre gehēt’ ‘fairly promised’. The manuscript has ‘leana’, then a gap, then ‘lēodū’ (folio 194b); the missing word, here ‘(mid)’, is supplied in different ways (Kemble ‘on’, Grein ‘his’, Grundtvig and four others ‘mid’, as printed here, Heyne and others ‘fore’ or ‘for’); ‘rewards among the people’ rests on ‘mid’, a guess. The ‘e’ at the end of ‘gelǣste’ is Klaeber’s change from ‘gelæsta’: ‘gelǣstan’ is ‘perform, fulfil’.

sentences.t:
geald þone gūðrǣs Gēata dryhten,
Hrēðles eafora, þā hē tō hām becōm,
Iofore ond Wulfe mid ofermāðmum,
sealde hiora gehwæðrum hund þūsenda
landes ond locenra bēaga,
sentences.l: The lord of the Geats, Hrethel’s heir, repaid that war-rush, when he came home, to Eofor and Wulf with over-treasures; gave to each of them a hundred thousand of land and of linked rings,
sentences.i: The lord of the Geats, Hrethel’s son, repaid that rush of battle when he came home: to Eofor and to Wulf he gave great treasures, and to each of them land and linked rings to the worth of a hundred thousand,
sentences.n: ‘Geald … gūðrǣs’ is ‘repaid the war-rush’ (‘gieldan’ with the accusative), and ‘Gēata dryhten, Hrēðles eafora’ ‘lord of the Geats, Hrethel’s heir’ is Higelac. ‘Iofore ond Wulfe’ is a dative, ‘to Eofor and Wulf’, and ‘mid ofermāðmum’ ‘with over-treasures’ (‘ofer-’, ‘surpassing’). ‘Hund þūsenda’ is ‘a hundred thousand’; Klaeber’s text does not name the unit, and I take it as a sum in value, ‘of land and of linked rings’ (‘locenra’ ‘of locked, linked’), which is a guess. ‘Hiora gehwæðrum’ is ‘to each of them’.

sentences.t:
— ne ðorfte him ðā lēan oðwītan
mon on middangearde, syðða[n] hīe ðā mǣrða geslōgon;
sentences.l: — not needed anyone on middle-earth to reproach them then with the reward, since they struck out those glories;
sentences.i: — and no man on earth had need to grudge them that reward, since they had won such fame by their blows;
sentences.n: Klaeber’s dash and semicolon bracket a side remark; Bugge set the part from ‘ne ðorfte’ to ‘middangearde’ (2995b–2996a) in parentheses. ‘Ne ðorfte … oðwītan’ is ‘had no need to reproach’; ‘oðwītan’ takes a dative of the person and an accusative of the thing, so ‘him … ðā lēan’ is ‘them … the reward’. I take ‘him’ as Eofor and Wulf; it could also be the king, and the sense then is that no one need blame him for giving it. A guess. ‘Ðā’ before ‘lēan’ I take as “then” (as in the literal line above), though it could be the plural article, ‘those rewards’. ‘Mon on middangearde’ is ‘a man on middle-earth’, the world. ‘Syðða[n]’ has its last ‘n’ added; ‘mǣrða geslōgon’ is ‘struck (won) glories’ by fighting.

sentences.t:
ond ðā Iofore forgeaf āngan dohtor,
hāmweorðunge, hyldo tō wedde.
sentences.l: and then to Eofor he gave his only daughter, a home-honouring, as pledge of favour.
sentences.i: And he gave his only daughter to Eofor, an honour for Eofor’s house, as a pledge of his favour.
sentences.n: ‘Forgeaf āngan dohtor’ is ‘gave (his) only daughter’, ‘āngan’ ‘only’, an accusative. ‘Hāmweorðunge’ is ‘home-honouring’, which I take as an honour to Eofor’s house (a guess from the two parts, ‘hām’ and ‘weorðung’). ‘Hyldo tō wedde’ is ‘as a pledge of favour’ (‘wedd’ ‘pledge’, ‘hyldo’ the genitive or accusative of ‘hyldu’, ‘favour’).

sentences.t:
Þæt ys sīo fǣhðo ond se fēondscipe,
wælnīð wera, ðæs ðe ic [wēn] hafo,
þē ūs sēceað tō Swēona lēoda,
sentences.l: That is the feud and the enmity, the slaughter-hate of men, as I expect, which seek us out from the Swedes’ people,
sentences.i: That is the feud and the hostility, the deadly hatred between men, and, as I expect, it will come to us from the Swedish people,
sentences.n: The messenger now turns from the old war to what he expects. ‘Þæt ys sīo fǣhðo ond se fēondscipe, wælnīð wera’ is ‘that is the feud and the enmity, the slaughter-hate of men’. ‘Ðæs ðe ic [wēn] hafo’ is ‘as I have expectation’; ‘wēn’ is Kemble’s addition. ‘Þē ūs sēceað tō Swēona lēoda’ is the hard part: ‘þē’ is ‘which’, ‘sēceað’ is plural (so the feud and enmity together are its subject), ‘ūs sēceað’ is ‘seek us out’, and ‘tō Swēona lēoda’ I take as ‘from the Swedes’ people’, with ‘lēoda’ the genitive plural of ‘lēod’; the case and the use of ‘tō’ are doubtful (Kemble and others print ‘lēode’). I follow the sense, that the Swedes will come at the Geats, and leave the grammar a guess.

sentences.t:
syððan hīe gefricgeað frēan ūserne
ealdorlēasne, þone ðe ǣr gehēold
wið hettendum hord ond rīce,
sentences.l: after they learn of our lord lifeless, him who formerly held against the haters hoard and kingdom,
sentences.i: as soon as they learn that our lord is dead, the man who once held hoard and kingdom against his foes,
sentences.n: ‘Syððan hīe gefricgeað’ is ‘after they learn’ (a present plural, ‘gefricgan’, ‘learn by hearing’), with the accusative ‘frēan ūserne ealdorlēasne’, ‘our lord lifeless’. ‘Ealdorlēas’ has ‘ealdor’ in its sense of ‘life’; the same word can mean ‘lordless’, but ‘frēan’ already names the lord. ‘Þone ðe ǣr gehēold’ is ‘him who formerly held’, and ‘wið hettendum’ ‘against haters’, that is, foes; ‘hord ond rīce’ is ‘hoard and kingdom’.

sentences.t:
æfter hæleða hryre, hwate Sǣ-Gēatas,
folcrēd fremede, oððe furður gēn
eorlscipe efnde.
sentences.l: after the fall of heroes, the bold Sea-Geats, [he] performed the people’s counsel, or yet further performed noble-deed.
sentences.i: and who, after the fall of the heroes, the bold Geats, did what served the people, or went further still and did a nobleman’s deeds.
sentences.n: ‘Æfter hæleða hryre, hwate Sǣ-Gēatas’ is ‘after the fall of heroes, the bold Sea-Geats’, with ‘hwate Sǣ-Gēatas’ in apposition to ‘hæleða’, as in ‘æfter hæleþa hryre, hwate Scyldungas’ at 2052; the apposition is loose, since ‘hæleða’ is genitive and ‘Sǣ-Gēatas’ nominative. ‘Fremede’ and ‘efnde’ are singular, so their subject is ‘þone ðe ǣr gehēold’ of the line before, Beowulf, not the Sea-Geats: ‘folcrēd fremede’ is ‘performed the people’s counsel’, what served the people, and ‘oððe furður gēn eorlscipe efnde’ ‘or yet further performed noble-deed’, as ‘eorlscipe efnde’ at 2133. The manuscript has ‘scildingas’; the italic ‘Sǣ-Gēat’ is Klaeber’s change, following an article in JEGPh; Heyne reads ‘Scilfingas’ (‘Scylfings’), as do Holthausen and Sedgefield, who also move the line to follow 3001, and one editor reads ‘hæleðes’; the line is therefore uncertain.

sentences.t:
— Nū is ofọst betost,
þæt wē þēodcyning þǣr scēawian,
ond þone gebringan, þē ūs bēagas geaf,
on ādfære.
sentences.l: — Now is haste best, that we go look upon the people-king there, and bring him, who gave us rings, on the pyre-journey.
sentences.i: — Now it is best that we hurry to look upon our king there and bring him, the giver of our rings, on his way to the fire.
sentences.n: ‘Nū is ofọst betost, þæt wē … scēawian’ is ‘now haste is best, that we look’. The ‘Nū’ is Klaeber’s italic: the manuscript has ‘me’, and Kemble gave ‘Nū’. ‘Ofọst’ has the metre dot again. ‘Þēodcyning’ is ‘people-king’; ‘þone gebringan, þē ūs bēagas geaf’ is ‘and bring him, who gave us rings’. ‘On ādfære’ is ‘on the pyre-journey’ (‘ād’ ‘pyre’, ‘fær’ ‘journey’), his last trip, to the fire.

sentences.t:
Ne scel ānes hwæt
meltan mid þām mōdịgan,
sentences.l: Not shall a single something melt with the proud-minded one,
sentences.i: Not one small thing only shall melt away with the bold king,
sentences.n: ‘Ne scel ānes hwæt meltan’ is ‘not shall a single something melt’: ‘ānes hwæt’ is ‘of one something’. Because the next lines say that the fire shall devour the treasure, I take the clause as ‘not one thing only’, in the pattern ‘not … but’; the sense is a guess. ‘Meltan’ is ‘melt’, here burn, as gold in a pyre. ‘Mid þām mōdịgan’ is ‘with the proud-minded one’, Beowulf, in the dative; the dot under ‘ị’ is again the metre sign.

sentences.t:
ac þǣr is māðma hord,
gold unrīme grimme gecēa(po)d,
ond nū æt sīðestan sylfes fēore
bēagas (geboh)te;
sentences.l: but there is a hoard of treasures, gold beyond count, grimly bought, and now at the last, with his own life, he bought rings;
sentences.i: But there is a hoard of treasures, gold past counting, bought at a grim price; and now at the last he has bought rings with his own life;
sentences.n: ‘Gecēa(po)d’ is ‘bought’, the past participle of ‘gecēapian’, with ‘grimme’ ‘grimly’ (an adverb, or a dative, ‘at a grim price’, as in the idiomatic line); the letters in parentheses are lost where the manuscript is burned and were filled in by Kemble. ‘Æt sīðestan’ is ‘at the last’, ‘sylfes fēore’ ‘with his own life’ (a dative of price). The verb ‘(geboh)te’, ‘bought’, is likewise restored (Grundtvig’s edition has ‘(geboh)te’; his transcript has ‘(beboh)te’), and the subject, Beowulf, is not named.

sentences.t:
þā sceall brond fretan,
ǣled þeccean,
sentences.l: these shall a brand devour, fire cover,
sentences.i: The fire shall devour them, flames shall cover them,
sentences.n: ‘Þā’ is ‘them’, the rings and treasure; ‘brond’ is ‘firebrand’ and ‘ǣled’ ‘fire’, both subjects, with the infinitives ‘fretan’ ‘devour’ and ‘þeccean’ ‘cover’ after ‘sceall’. The messenger proposes to burn the treasure with the king, not to share it out.

sentences.t:
— nalles eorl wegan
māððum tō gemyndum, nē mægð scȳne
habban on healse hringweorðunge,
sentences.l: — not at all shall an earl bear treasure for remembrance, nor a fair maiden have on her neck ring-adornment,
sentences.i: — no warrior shall bear away a treasure as a memorial, and no fair maiden shall wear a ring-adornment at her throat,
sentences.n: The dash carries ‘sceall’ over from the previous clause: nothing shall be borne away. ‘Nalles eorl wegan māððum tō gemyndum’ is ‘not at all shall an earl bear treasure for remembrance’; Holthausen and Trautmann read ‘þicgean’, ‘receive’, for ‘wegan’, ‘bear’. ‘Mægð scȳne’ is ‘fair maiden’, and ‘on healse hringweorðunge’ ‘on her neck ring-adornment’, ‘healse’ a dative.

sentences.t:
ac sceal geōmormōd, golde berēafod
oft nalles ǣne elland tredan,
sentences.l: but shall, sad-minded, bereft of gold, often, not once, tread a foreign land,
sentences.i: but, sad at heart and robbed of gold, he must walk a strange land again and again,
sentences.n: ‘Ac sceal … elland tredan’ is ‘but shall tread a foreign land’, with the earl of the line before as its unnamed subject. ‘Geōmormōd, golde berēafod’ is ‘sad-minded, bereft of gold’, and ‘oft nalles ǣne’ ‘often, not once’, a way of saying ‘many times, and not just the once’. ‘Elland’ is ‘foreign land’, the exile that follows the lord’s death.

sentences.t:
nū se herewīsa hleahtor ālegde,
gamen ond glēodrēam.
sentences.l: now that the army-wise one has laid down laughter, game and glee-joy.
sentences.i: now that our wise war-leader has put away laughter, play and the joy of song.
sentences.n: ‘Nū’ is ‘now that’, and ‘se herewīsa’ ‘the army-wise one’, Beowulf, who ‘hleahtor ālegde’, ‘laid down laughter’. ‘Gamen ond glēodrēam’ are two more objects, ‘game’ (play) and ‘glee-joy’, ‘glēo’ being music or minstrelsy, as in ‘glēobēam’ ‘glee-wood’ at 2263.

sentences.t:
Forðon sceall gār wesan
monig morgenceald mundum bewunden,
hæfen on handa,
sentences.l: Therefore shall spear be many a one morning-cold, wound about by hands, lifted in the hand,
sentences.i: Therefore many a spear, cold in the morning, shall be grasped in hands and lifted in the hand,
sentences.n: ‘Forðon sceall gār wesan … bewunden’ is ‘therefore shall many a spear be wound about’, with ‘mundum’ ‘by hands’ (dative of means) and ‘hæfen on handa’ ‘lifted in the hand’. ‘Monig morgenceald’ is ‘many a one morning-cold’, spears taken up in the chill of daybreak; the poem does not say when the fighting is to be.

sentences.t:
nalles hearpan swēg
wīgend weccean,
sentences.l: not at all shall the sound of the harp wake the warriors,
sentences.i: and no harp’s sound shall wake the warriors,
sentences.n: ‘Nalles hearpan swēg wīgend weccean’ is ‘not at all shall the sound of the harp wake warriors’. Harp and spear are set against each other: ‘hearpan’ is genitive singular, ‘wīgend’ an accusative plural.

sentences.t:
ac se wonna hrefn
fūs ofer fǣgum fela reordian,
earne secgan, hū him æt ǣte spēow,
sentences.l: but the dark raven, eager over the doomed, shall say much, tell the eagle how it fared with him at the eating,
sentences.i: but the dark raven, greedy above the doomed, shall have much to say and tell the eagle how well it went with him at the feast,
sentences.n: ‘Se wonna hrefn’ is ‘the dark raven’, and ‘fūs ofer fǣgum’ ‘eager over the doomed’ (‘fǣge’, as in ‘fǣge’ at 2975). ‘Fela reordian’ is ‘speak much’ (‘reord’ ‘voice’). ‘Earne secgan’ is ‘tell the eagle’, a dative. ‘Hū him æt ǣte spēow’ is ‘how it succeeded for him at the eating’: ‘spēow’ is the past of ‘spōwan’ and takes the dative. Raven, eagle and wolf are the usual beasts of the battlefield in Old English verse, and the eagle prepares the name of the headland at 3031.

sentences.t: þenden hē wið wulf[e] wæl rēafode.’
sentences.l: while he, with the wolf, plundered the slain.’
sentences.i: while he and the wolf stripped the dead.’
sentences.n: ‘Þenden hē wið wulf[e] wæl rēafode’ is ‘while he, together with the wolf, plundered the slain’: ‘wið’ takes the dative, ‘wulf[e]’, and ‘wæl’ is ‘the slain’. The final ‘e’ is added (the manuscript has ‘wulf’). The closing quotation mark ends the messenger’s speech, which began at 2900.

sentences.t:
Swā se secg hwata secggende wæs
lāðra spella;
sentences.l: So the bold man was telling of loathly tidings;
sentences.i: So the brave man spoke, telling of hateful happenings;
sentences.n: ‘Swā se secg hwata secggende wæs’ is ‘so the bold man was telling’: ‘secggende’ is a present participle and takes the genitive ‘lāðra spella’, ‘of hateful tidings’. Grein and others join ‘secg hwata’ into one word, ‘secghwata’, ‘the bold man’; the sense is the same.

sentences.t:
hē ne lēag fela
wyrda nē worda.
sentences.l: he did not lie much of fates nor of words.
sentences.i: he told few lies about what had happened or what was said.
sentences.n: ‘Hē ne lēag fela wyrda nē worda’ is ‘he did not lie much of fates or of words’; ‘wyrda’ and ‘worda’ are partitive genitives. The litotes means he told it nearly all as it was.

sentences.t: Weorod eall ārās;
sentences.l: The troop all arose;
sentences.i: The whole company rose;
sentences.n: ‘Ārās’ is the past of ‘ārīsan’, ‘arise’, and ‘weorod eall’ ‘the whole troop’, singular noun with ‘eall’. The short clause marks the move from words to action.

sentences.t:
ēodon unblīðe under Earnanæs,
wollentēare wundur scēawian.
sentences.l: they went unblithe under Earnanæs, with welling tears, to behold the wonder.
sentences.i: they went, joyless and weeping, beneath Earnanæs to look at the marvel.
sentences.n: ‘Ēodon unblīðe’ is ‘went unblithe’, with ‘wollentēare’ (‘wollen’, ‘welling’, + ‘tēar’), ‘weeping’, an adjective. ‘Earnanæs’ is ‘eagle-headland’, ‘earna’ the genitive of ‘earn’, ‘eagle’; ‘under’ places them at its foot. ‘Wundur scēawian’ is ‘to behold the wonder’.

sentences.l: They found then on the sand, soulless, holding the couch, him who gave them rings in earlier times;
sentences.i: There on the sand they found him lifeless on his bed, the man who had given them rings in earlier days;
sentences.n: ‘Fundon … sāwullēasne … healdan’ is ‘found … soulless … holding’; ‘sāwullēasne’ is an accusative singular, ‘soulless’. ‘Hlimbed’ is a rare word, which I take as ‘couch, bed’; the first element is not clear (a guess). ‘Þone þe him hringas geaf’ is ‘him who gave them rings’, and ‘ǣrran mǣlum’ ‘at earlier times’ (the apparatus says Zupitza read ‘ærrun’, the ‘u’ altered from ‘a’ by erasure, and Sedgefield and Chambers ‘ærran’, the ‘a’ partly obliterated, so the reading is partly doubtful).

sentences.t:
þā wæs endedæg
gōdum gegongen, þæt se gūðcyning,
Wedra þēoden wundọrdēaðe swealt.
sentences.l: then was the end-day gone upon the good one, in that the war-king, the Weders’ prince, died a wonder-death.
sentences.i: Now the day of his end had come upon the good king, the war-king, prince of the Weders, who died a death of wonder.
sentences.n: ‘Endedæg gōdum gegongen’ is ‘end-day gone to the good one’: ‘gegongen’ is a participle, ‘gōdum’ a dative. ‘Þæt’ introduces the fact, ‘that the war-king died’. ‘Gūðcyning’ is ‘war-king’ and ‘Wedra þēoden’ ‘Weders’ prince’, both Beowulf. In ‘wundọrdēaðe’ the dot under ‘ọ’ is the metre sign; the word is a dative, ‘a wonder-death’, a death that came through a marvel, the dragon.

sentences.l: Before that, they saw there a stranger creature, the worm on the plain, in the opposite place, loathly lying;
sentences.i: Before that, they had seen a stranger creature there, the dragon lying hateful on the plain, right across from them;
sentences.n: ‘Ǣr hī þǣr gesēgan syllīcran wiht’ is ‘before they saw there a stranger creature’: ‘syllīcran’ is a comparative, ‘more strange’. The word ‘ǣr’ is disputed: Thorpe reads ‘ac’ (‘but’), Grundtvig ‘ǣc’ (‘also’), Bugge drops ‘þǣr’, and Sievers and others read ‘þǣr hī þā’; I take ‘ǣr’ as ‘before (they came to the king)’, a guess. ‘Wyrm … lāðne licgean’ is ‘the worm lying loathly’, ‘lāðne’ an accusative, and ‘wiðerræhtes’ ‘opposite, against’. ‘Wyrm’ is ‘worm’ in ‘l’ and ‘dragon’ in ‘i’, by the house rule.

sentences.t:
wæs se lēgdraca
grimlīc gry(refāh) glēdum beswǣled;
sentences.l: the flame-dragon was grim-looking, terror-coloured, scorched with embers;
sentences.i: the fire-dragon was a fearful sight, dreadfully stained, and scorched with embers;
sentences.n: ‘Lēgdraca’ is ‘flame-dragon’ (‘lēg’ ‘flame’). ‘Grimlīc’ is ‘grim-looking’. The word ‘gry(refāh)’ is restored: the manuscript breaks off after ‘gry’ at the end of a page, with room for about five letters (Chambers); Thorkelin read ‘gryre’, Heyne ‘gryregæst’, and Bugge, Sedgefield and Chambers ‘gryrefāh’, ‘terror-coloured’. I follow them; the letters are a guess. ‘Glēdum beswǣled’ is ‘scorched with embers’, ‘beswǣlan’ ‘to burn’, and ‘glēdum’ the dative of ‘glēd’, ‘ember’.

sentences.t:
sē wæs fīftiges fōtgemearces
lang on legere;
sentences.l: he was fifty foot-measures long where he lay;
sentences.i: he measured fifty feet as he lay;
sentences.n: ‘Fīftiges fōtgemearces’ is ‘of fifty foot-measure’, a genitive of measure with ‘lang’, so ‘fifty feet long’. ‘On legere’ is ‘in the lying, where he lay’.

sentences.l: he held the air-joy at times by night, went down again to seek his den;
sentences.i: by night, from time to time, he took his joy of the air, and went down again to seek his den;
sentences.n: ‘Lyftwynne hēold’ is ‘held the air-joy’, the pleasure of flying, and ‘nihtes hwīlum’ ‘by night at times’, genitive of time with an adverb. ‘Nyðer eft gewāt’ is ‘went down again’. ‘Dennes nīosian’ is ‘to seek out the den’: ‘nīosian’ takes the genitive (Holthausen and Schücking read ‘nīosan’).

sentences.t:
wæs ðā dēaðe fæst,
hæfde eorðscrafa ende genyttod.
sentences.l: he was then fast in death, had used the end of earth-caves.
sentences.i: Now he was held fast by death, and had had the last use of his earth-caves.
sentences.n: ‘Dēaðe fæst’ is ‘fast in death’ (as ‘dēaðbedde fæst’ at 2901). ‘Hæfde … ende genyttod’ is ‘had used up the end’: ‘genyttian’ is ‘use, have the use of’, so the dragon has had his last turn of the ‘eorðscrafa’, ‘earth-caves’ (‘scrafu’, a cave, dug place). The sense, ‘come to the end of his use of them’, is from the lexica and the context.

sentences.t:
Him big stōdan bunan ond orcas,
discas lāgon ond dȳre swyrd,
sentences.l: By him stood beakers and flagons, dishes lay and precious swords,
sentences.i: By him stood cups and flagons; dishes lay there, and costly swords,
sentences.n: ‘Him big stōdan’ is ‘by him stood’; ‘big’ is ‘by, beside’ (‘bī’). ‘Bunan ond orcas’ are two kinds of vessel (‘bune’ I take as ‘cup, beaker’; ‘orc’ as ‘flagon’; both are guesses from the glossary), and ‘discas’ are dishes. ‘Dȳre swyrd’ is ‘precious swords’.

sentences.t:
ōmige þurhetone, swā hīe wið eorðan fæðm
þūsend wintra þǣr eardodon;
sentences.l: rusty, eaten through, as if they in the earth’s embrace a thousand winters there had dwelt;
sentences.i: rusted and eaten through, as if they had lain a thousand winters there in the grasp of the earth;
sentences.n: ‘Ōmige’ is ‘rusty’ (‘ōm’ ‘rust’; Scheinert reads ‘ōme’ with a query), and ‘þurhetone’ ‘eaten through’, the participle of ‘þurhetan’. ‘Swā hīe … eardodon’ is ‘as if they had dwelt’ (the plural ending ‘-odon’ is the same in the indicative and the subjunctive; the ‘as if’ is from the sense of ‘swā’). ‘Wið eorðan fæðm’ is ‘in the earth’s embrace’ (‘fæðm’ ‘embrace, grasp’). ‘Þūsend wintra’ is ‘a thousand winters’, a long time, stated as the poet’s round number.

sentences.t:
þonne wæs þæt yrfe ēacencræftig,
iūmonna gold galdre bewunden,
sentences.l: for that treasure was exceedingly powerful, the gold of men of old, wound about with a spell,
sentences.i: for that wealth was of mighty power, the gold of the men of old, bound round with a charm,
sentences.n: ‘Þonne’ I take as ‘for’ or ‘then’; the spell of the next line is why no man might touch the hall (3053). ‘Yrfe’ is ‘inheritance, treasure’, ‘ēacencræftig’ ‘enormously powerful’ (‘ēacen’ ‘increased, huge’, a rare word), and ‘iūmonna gold’ ‘the gold of men of old’ (‘iū’ ‘formerly’, with ‘mon’ in the genitive plural). ‘Galdre bewunden’ is ‘wound about with a spell’; ‘galdor’ is a chant or charm, the curse laid on the hoard.

sentences.t:
þæt ðām hringsele hrīnan ne mōste
gumena ǣnig, nefne God sylfa,
sentences.l: so that to that ring-hall none of men might touch, except God himself,
sentences.i: so that no man at all might touch that ring-hall, unless God himself,
sentences.n: ‘Þæt ðām hringsele hrīnan ne mōste gumena ǣnig’ is ‘that none of men might touch the ring-hall’: ‘hrīnan’ takes the dative ‘ðām hringsele’, and ‘gumena ǣnig’ is ‘any of men’. ‘Hringsele’ is ‘ring-hall’ (‘hringsele’ at 2840), here the barrow’s chamber of treasure. ‘Nefne God sylfa’ is ‘except God himself’, and the clause goes on in the next unit.

sentences.t:
sigora Sōðcyning sealde þām ðe hē wolde
— hē is manna gehyld — hord openian,
sentences.l: the true king of victories, should give to whom he would — he is the protector of men — to open the hoard,
sentences.i: the true King of victories, were to grant to the man he chose — he is the protector of mankind — leave to open the hoard,
sentences.n: ‘Sigora Sōðcyning’ is ‘true king of victories’ (compare ‘sigora Waldend’ at 2875). ‘Sealde’ is a past subjunctive after ‘nefne’, ‘should give’, with ‘þām ðe hē wolde’ ‘to him whom he would’ and ‘hord openian’ ‘to open the hoard’. ‘Hē is manna gehyld’ is ‘he is protector of men’: ‘gehyld’ is ‘protection, guardian’. Grundtvig (with a query) and Bugge read ‘gehyht’ (‘hope’), and Bugge and others ‘hæleða’ for ‘manna’; Holthausen and Sedgefield set the order ‘gehyld manna’.

sentences.t: efne swā hwylcum manna, swā him gemet ðūhte.
sentences.l: even to whichever of men, as seemed fitting to him.
sentences.i: even to whichever man seemed right to him.
sentences.n: ‘Efne swā hwylcum manna’ is ‘even to whichever of men’, ‘manna’ a partitive genitive after ‘hwylcum’. ‘Swā him gemet ðūhte’ is ‘as to him fitting seemed’: ‘ðūhte’ is the past of ‘ðyncan’ and takes the dative, and ‘gemet’ is ‘fitting’ (I take it as a noun, ‘what is fitting’). The sentence leaves the choice of who may open the hoard to God.
